# Discussion

Across a matched national design and four independent estimators (cross-sectional irrigated-area
expansion and ET buffering, and forcing-interacted slope gaps on observed area and ET), the
operational effect of reservoirs on drought outcomes brackets zero once siting is matched out. The
same answer holds for the direct, vegetation-independent availability outcome: the apparent
flattening of meteorological-to-streamflow drought propagation in dammed basins is as strong at
physically unregulated *upstream* reaches as downstream, and collapses from a slope gap of $-0.18$
to ≈$-0.03$ when the comparison is made within climate region. Dammed basins do hold roughly
4.6 times more cropland than matched controls (11.1% vs 2.4% of basin area), but this gap is fixed across the record,
with parallel pre-trends and no divergence through the megadrought. Taken together, the evidence
supports a single interpretation: reservoirs **mark** where water-dependent vulnerability already
concentrated (arid, already-irrigated basins), rather than **make** it. The vulnerability
signature is a property of siting, set before the drought and stable through it, not a dynamic
consequence of regulation.

This reframes "no effect" as the finding rather than a failure of power, but only because a
credible *cause* of the apparent effect is identified. The within-basin upstream/downstream placebo
is the cleanest within-design falsification here: a genuine regulation effect must appear downstream
of the dam and be absent upstream, and it is not. What remains, once that placebo and within-region conditioning are applied,
is the aridity gradient itself. The methodological corollary is general. A naive dammed–control
contrast, or a calendar-time difference-in-differences, would read the large cross-sectional area,
ET, and transmission gaps (amplified during the drought) as a reservoir effect; conditioning on
realized meteorological forcing and estimating a deficit-to-impact *slope*, and benchmarking against
an unregulated within-basin reach, makes the signal disappear. Reservoir-buffering studies that
compare dammed against undammed basins, or pre- against post-construction levels, inherit the full
siting confound [@lopezmoreno_dam_2009; @wu_non-linear_2017; @wu_impacts_2018; @schilstra_effects_2024; @lee_drought_2026];
the upstream placebo is a transferable identification tool applicable to any regulated river with
gauges above and below the structure.

If reservoirs neither buffer nor amplify drought operationally, the relevant change under a
multi-decadal dry spell is in the water available to store rather than in the structures, and the
storage record is suggestive on this point. The seasonal refill remains efficient and its amplitude
is unchanged, yet the entire storage band drifts downward, peak and trough declining in step at
roughly $-1.3$ and $-1.2$ percentage points of capacity per year. A band that drops without
narrowing is consistent with a falling supply ceiling rather than a degraded buffer. We stress that
this is a descriptive, control-free trend that cannot on its own separate declining inflow from
rising demand-side drawdown [@condon_evapotranspiration_2020]; both would shift the band downward
without narrowing it. Our most direct demand proxy, however, weighs against the demand explanation:
irrigated area in dammed basins did not expand over the period (stable, parallel trajectories; a
differential-expansion ATT indistinguishable from zero), so rising consumptive demand is not
evident as the driver, even though a crop-composition shift toward more water-intensive perennials
could raise per-area use without enlarging area. Read against
Chile's documented transition from episodic drought toward structural aridification (in which
declining precipitation and rising atmospheric evaporative demand lower inflows independently of any
infrastructure [@zambrano_drought_2025; @Vicente-Serrano2022; @vicenteserrano_unraveling_2019; @garreaud_20102015_2017; @AlvarezGarreton2021],
echoing aridification trajectories documented elsewhere [@overpeck_climate_2020])
and the global pattern in which reservoirs increasingly fail to refill and the storage returns of
new dam construction are diminishing [@wang_reservoir_2024; @li_diminishing_2023], the more likely
reading is that the binding constraint is shifting toward water supply rather than storage capacity
or operation. A naturalized-inflow series and a demand-side decomposition are needed to settle this,
and we treat it as a strong hypothesis rather than an identified result.

The policy implication is direct and uncomfortable for the prevailing response to scarcity in Chile
and elsewhere. Because the 1981 Water Code makes existing water-use rights perpetual private
property that the state cannot readily curtail during drought, the reflexive response has been
supply-side, a national programme of new dams and inter-basin transfers
[@Barria2021; @Garreaud2025; @macpherson_evolving_2023]. Our results imply that adding storage to
basins whose inflow is declining is a supply-blind response to a supply problem: it cannot
manufacture water that aridification is removing, and the buffering benefit it is built to provide
is, on this evidence, attributable to where dams sit rather than to what they do. This is the
drought-domain expression of the reservoir-effect and supply–demand-cycle hypotheses
[@di_baldassarre_water_2018], whose practical force has been contested for want of quantification
[@kellner_controversial_2021]; we provide a credibly identified test and find the protective
function over-attributed. The leverage instead lies on the demand and allocation side (curbing the
over-allocation and induced expansion that the efficiency paradox entrenches
[@grafton_paradox_2018; @reade_malagueno_libre_2024; @jordan_adaptation_2025]) and in managed
recharge and reallocation rather than new impoundments
[@rivera-vidal_managed_2025; @rivera_legal_2016; @scanlon_global_2023].

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, treatment is effectively time-invariant over
the record (most reservoirs predate it), so we identify differential drought *response* rather than
the effect of switching a reservoir on; a staggered-commissioning design is infeasible here and
would be the cleaner counterfactual where construction dates and longer records permit. Second, the
result is a bounded null, not a proven equivalence: with ~21 treated clusters the design rules out
buffering larger than ≈46–58% of baseline transmission for streamflow but cannot exclude small
operational effects, so the causal weight rests on the placebo, not on equivalence. Third, the
observed-area outcome (MapBiomas class 18) captures total cropland rather than irrigation status,
and Chile's agricultural change has been compositional (a shift toward perennial orchards within
roughly constant cropland area), so a latent water-demand signal not visible in net area remains
possible; whole-basin MODIS ET is additionally confounded by residual aridity over barren land, so
the ET conclusion leans on the cross-sectional buffering null and the orchard stratum, both
low-powered (minimum detectable effects of roughly twice their baselines), so for ET specifically
the finding is "no *large* effect detected" rather than no effect. Relatedly,
the matched set leaves baseline aridity imbalanced (SMD ≈0.17), so the doubly-robust adjustment for
it is load-bearing and the estimates are sensitive to its functional form: a quadratic aridity term
moves the proxy transmission-slope estimate from $+0.33$ to $+0.11$, toward the null we report, and
a reminder that the linear-adjustment values are not the conservative ones. Fourth, the
streamflow placebo covers 15 of 21 treated basins over 2000–2020, and the high-supply southern
subset is small; a modest regulation effect in wetter basins cannot be excluded, though drought is
also least binding there. Upstream and downstream gauges are also not perfectly interchangeable
(upstream gauges sit higher, and elevation predicts the transmission slope among controls), so a
residual regime component remains; that said, the raw upstream and downstream transmission slopes
are nearly identical and the apparent buffering is if anything stronger upstream, neither of which
is consistent with a regulation effect obscured by elevation. The 12-month aggregation is a further
boundary: it targets annual-to-interannual transmission and does not resolve the sub-seasonal
(1–3 month) operational buffering reservoirs are designed to provide, so our conclusions concern
long-term vulnerability rather than short-term operation. Generalizability is also bounded by
governance: Chile's 1981 Water Code is an unusually extreme, market-based regime (perpetual,
tradable private rights the state cannot readily curtail), so while the *operational* finding
(that buffering reflects siting, not regulation) should hold wherever dam siting is non-random, the
demand-feedback and policy inferences are conditioned on this weak adaptive feedback; under
state-managed or dynamically regulated allocation, operators able to curtail demand or re-time
releases could in principle produce genuine buffering, or weaker induced-demand lock-in, than we
observe here. Finally, residual SUTVA spillovers (adjacency, shared aquifers) survive
the contamination rule, and our estimand is the *drought* effect of reservoirs, not their value for
hydropower, flood control, or urban supply, which this study does not assess.

One alternative interpretation deserves emphasis because mean-based estimators cannot see it:
damming might leave the *magnitude* of drought impact unchanged while recomposing its
**dependence structure**, weakening the meteorology→outcome coupling and substituting a
storage→outcome coupling, a regime shift that would itself explain the convergent null. We cannot
adjudicate this with the present data: the storage-recovery dynamics are stationary (refill
efficiency and amplitude are flat), which weakens the premise, and the decisive test requires
reservoir release and operating-rule records that set storage *independently* of contemporaneous
inflow. The only storage signal on disk is monthly change in storage (a drawdown proxy), which is
an endogenous hydrological response to the same precipitation and inflow forcing (and partly to
demand) and is therefore collinear with SPEI; regressing an outcome on it cannot separate a
genuine storage→outcome regime from the forcing→outcome coupling we already estimate, because it
carries no independent allocation information. Identifying the dependence-shift limb thus needs
exogenous release or rule-curve data. Absent that, and given that any apparent decoupling must
survive the upstream placebo, the dependence-shift account reduces to the siting interpretation. Resolving it (together
with longer streamflow records and water-rights allocation data) is the priority for future work.

Returning to the question that motivates the study (do reservoirs create resilience or merely
postpone vulnerability under prolonged drought?), our evidence indicates that, under aridification,
they do neither operationally: storage neither buffers nor amplifies the drought signal beyond what
basin siting already implies, while the water available to store steadily declines. Resilience to a
falling supply ceiling will not come from more impoundments but from confronting demand and
allocation, the harder, and unavoidable, adaptation.

# Data and code availability

The full analysis pipeline, comprising the `targets` workflow, the reusable R functions (`src/R/`), the
study-parameter configuration (`config/`), and the scripts that generate every figure and table,
is openly available at <https://github.com/frzambra/dam_drought_effectiveness> and archived on
Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX). The pinned R environment
(`renv.lock`) reproduces the package versions used. Reservoir storage records, the derived result
tables, and matched-set metadata are included in the repository; the third-party input datasets are
publicly available from their providers as cited: CHIRPS/CHIRTS (standardized drought indices),
MODIS MOD16/MOD13/MOD17 (evapotranspiration and vegetation), MapBiomas Chile (land cover), the CR2
network (streamflow), SRTM (elevation), and the DGA reservoir and watershed registries. Every
result in the manuscript corresponds to a named pipeline target, so the analyses can be regenerated
with a single `targets::tar_make()`.
